summary.text: A previously healthy 12-year-old male was referred to the emergency department 7 days after ingestion of an unknown quantity of a liquid. Following the ingestion he had several episodes of vomiting, sometimes with bloody secretion, and anorexia, lethargy and discomfort during last week. On examination he was drowsy but arousal and afebrile. His oral mucosa was congested and edematous, with an exudative ulcerated tongue and edematous lip observed in the physical examination.

Initial complete blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, arterial blood gas, serum amylase and chest x-ray were normal or within normal limit. The electrocardiogram was normal and 2D echocardiography showed normal cardiac chambers with LVEF of 70%. Blood and urine cultures were sterile and serum urea was 212 mg/dL on the day of admission. He was diagnosed with acute paraquat poisoning; serum paraquat levels were not measured.

In the emergency he received IV fluid, ondansetron and ranitidine. Following admission to the hospital he received a Ventolin nebulizer, becotide spray, clindamycin, cloxacillin, ceftriaxone and pantoprazole, and nystatin drop was prescribed for the oral lesions. Kidney functions were seriously damaged 7 days following ingestion, and hemodialysis was done because of the continued increase in blood urea and creatinine.

Kidney functions gradually recovered completely 9 days later, and the patient was discharged after 9 days with BUN 19 mg/dL and Cr 1.3 mg/dL. He was followed a few weeks after discharge. The patient was cured, and the authors attribute his survival to vomiting the content of stomach readily after the ingestion, starting hemodialysis early after the admission and other interventions.
